entries.title: India news: India steps up efforts as hundreds missing in Nepal floods
entries.summary: India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi said he spoke with Nepal's Shah to offer humanitarian assistance. Meanwhile, India's RSS Chief Mohan Bhagwat is stirring up controversy in New York. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India steps up efforts as hundreds missing in Nepal floods

August 27, 2026

India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi said he spoke with Nepal's Shah to offer humanitarian assistance. Meanwhile, India's RSS Chief Mohan Bhagwat is stirring up controversy in New York. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Nepal's Foreign Minister says 300 Indian tourists are among the missing
  • Most were pilgrims on Mansarovar Yatra
  • India sends 10 metric tons of disaster-relief supplies to Nepal
  • US panel on religious freedom urges government to place sanctions on RSS members

Here are the biggest headlines coming out of India on Thursday, August 27:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section India sends more aid to Nepal while disaster personnel on standby

India sends more aid to Nepal while disaster personnel on standby

India has dispatched a second tranche of relief supplies to flood-affected Nepal on Thursday, External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar said.

"A second flight has just taken off, carrying 37.5 tonnes of HADR (Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief) material, medicines and food packets for Nepal," he said in a post on X, accompanied by a video which showed the material being loaded onto a military aircraft.

On Wednesday, India had sent 10 tonnes of aid material, including essential medicines.

However, no disaster relief team has been sent to sites so far, India's National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) IG Narendra Singh Bundela said in a press conference on Thursday morning.

"At present, no NDRF team has been sent to Nepal. Teams have been kept on standby. If a request is received from the Nepal government and the Government of India decides accordingly, an NDRF team will be sent," several media outlets reported him saying.

Indian Embassies in Nepal and China said they had set up helplines for information on Indian nationals impacted by the floods.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke with his Nepali counterpart Balendra Shah on Wednesday to express condolences on the lives lost. "India is prepared to provide Nepal with all possible types of humanitarian assistance. Our teams are closely coordinating on rescue and relief efforts," he had said in a post on X.

Skip next section Over 170 Indians missing in Nepal-Tibet floods

Over 170 Indians missing in Nepal-Tibet floods

More than 170 Indians were unaccounted for in the Nepal-Tibet flash floods, Nepal's tourism officials said on Thursday, as Indian authorities coordinated with their Nepalese counterparts on rescue and relief efforts. 

Nepal's police and tourism officials said that of the 800 tourists missing in the country, 177 were from India. Meanwhile, Nepal's Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal on Thursday said that over 300 Indian tourists were missing. He was speaking to journalists from Indian news channel NDTV World at the Anviksha Summit in Kathmandu.

"Foreign nationals, including Indians, take the route in the affected area to the Mansarovar Yatra. Close to 300 Indians have been reported missing and the government is trying to establish contact with them," Khanal said. Kailash Mansarovar is a high-altitude site in China's Tibet revered by Hindus and Buddhists.

At least 165 people have died in the flash floods which occurred at the Nepal-Tibet border on Wednesday. Over 1,300 were missing in both Nepal and Tibet. Nepal's police authorities have said they expect the death toll to rise.

Several Indian states have reported that dozens of their residents were among those missing in Nepal, as per local media reports.

Verified videos of the disaster showed massive masses of debris-laden water sweeping away dozens of people at various locations. The disaster has washed away homes and villages.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello! This is Mahima Kapoor from DW's Studio Delhi, bringing you the latest from across India.

More than 130 Indians are among the hundreds missing in Nepal's flash floods in what is being described as the country's worst disaster in years. The flood was triggered on Wednesday when an Avalanche reportedly blocked the flow of a tributary of the Bhotekoshi river. The river water swept away locals, pilgrims, proterties and whole villages in minutes.

India's central and state governments have sprung into action to account for their missing, coordinate information and send aid to the affected areas.

Meanwhile in the national capital, a student-led protest over an alleged suicide at the country's premier technology institute has entered its fourth day.

In other news, a US panel on religious freedom has urged the US government to consider targeted sanctions against the chief of a right-wing Hindu nationalist group closely associated with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

The panel's recommendation came days before the said chief is scheduled to speak at a private event in New York City's Madison Square Garden, which NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he opposes.

Stay tuned for all of this and more!

entries.title: Bundesliga season 2026-27: All you need to know
entries.summary: From key dates to rising football stars and changes, DW has the latest on the new Bundesliga season.
entries.content:
August 27, 2026

From key dates to rising football stars and changes, DW has the latest on the new Bundesliga season.

When does the new Bundesliga season start?

The 2026-27 Bundesliga season starts on August 28 with defending champions Bayern Munich at home against Stuttgart. Borussia Dortmund host Hamburg, while newcomers Elversberg start at home against Bayer Leverkusen.

The Women's Bundesliga began on August 21, as Bayern Munich defeated Union Berlin in the capital. Both Stuttgart and Mainz are new to the league this year, replacing Carl Zeiss Jena and Essen who were relegated.

As is custom in Germany, the domestic men's season truly begins for Bundesliga sides with the first round of the German Cup, which started the week before the league season. The biggest upset in the opening round was Heidenheim, who were in the Bundesliga last season, losing to fourth-division team Jeddeloh. Both Bayern and Dortmund will have to wait a bit longer to play their first round game because the two faced off in the German Super Cup (the game between the league and cup winners of the previous season) - where Bayern ran out winners.

The first 'Klassiker' of the new Bundesliga season is at the end of October and will be played in Munich.

The winter break starts after the 14th game of the season on December 20. The Bundesliga will resume play on the weekend of January 8 and has midweek games immediately afterwards.

Are there any new rules in the Bundesliga season?

Some of the new rules we saw at the World Cup will be applied in the Bundesliga too.

Measures are being introduced to improve time management, with the referees able to use the five-second countdown that was on show at the World Cup for goal kicks and throw ins. Although rarely seen, if the limit is exceeded a goal kick becomes a corner for the opposition and a throw in changes hands.

Substitutes will have 10 seconds to leave the pitch, otherwise the new player will have to wait until a break in play – at least a minute later – before he can return to the field.

VAR will also be allowed to have a say in second yellow cards and corner kicks. If a player covers his mouth during a dispute with an opponent, he may be punished with a yellow card. At the World Cup, this was punishable by a red card. Scheduled hydration breaks, regardless of the temperature, will not be introduced in the Bundesliga.

There will also be a new longer international break this season, which sees September's and October's breaks merge into one three-week break starting on September 24 and ending on October 4. This means Bundesliga action will pause for 16 days. The November international break will remain a nine-day interruption.

Have there been any major Bundesliga transfers?

There have been a few signings of real note this summer, perhaps most famously and unsurprisingly at Bayern Munich.

Breakout Germany wingback Nathaniel Brown signed from Frankfurt, while Moroccan striker Ismael Saibari also joins as a strong back-up to Harry Kane.

Elsewhere in the league, Dortmund signed Konstantinos Karetsas for a reported €30 million ($34.6 million) from KRC Genk. Gladbach's German midfield starlet Rocco Reitz left for RB Leipzig, while Hoffenheim are excited by the arrival of 18-year-old holding midfielder Nathan De Cat. Leverkusen reportedly spent €32 million on Afonso Moreira. The Portuguese left winger hopes to continue the form he showed at Lyon.

Freiburg have a new goalkeeper – Mio Backhaus signed from Werder Bremen. Noah Atubolu is expected to join Frankfurt.

The son of former England striker Emile Heskey, Reigan has signed for Cologne, and Robin Gosens returns to Germany to play for newly promoted Schalke.

There have also been a few departures from the league this season. After leaving Bayern Munich at the end of his contract earlier in the summer, Leon Goretzka is reportedly on the verge of joining Aston Villa in the Premier League. Former Borussia Dortmund defender Niklas Süle has retired, opting to play for fun in the lower leagues. Former Dortmund teammate Julian Brandt has moved to Ajax on a Bosman.

Bazoumana Toure leaves Hoffenheim after just a year at the club. The 20-year-old Ivorian winger left the Bundesliga for the Premier League, signing for Newcastle for reportedly a whopping €50 million.

Leverkusen moved on from Alejandro Grimaldo and Matej Kovar, while Freiburg's exciting Swiss midfielder Johan Manzambi moved to Aston Villa for a reported €60 million.

Who are the new teams and coaches in the Bundesliga?

For the first time since 2012, there will be three new teams in the Bundesliga. Elversberg become the 59th club in the history of the Bundesliga, while giants Schalke return after three years away. Paderborn won the playoff to also return, having been in the second division for six years. Wolfsburg lost that game, which saw them relegated for the first time in their history. St. Pauli and Heidenheim were the other two teams relegated.

There have been four coaching changes for the new season. Marie-Louise Eta, who was only in a caretaker role, is replaced full time by the Swiss Mauro Lustrinelli at Union Berlin. Albert Riera's disastrous run at Eintracht Frankfurt was unsurprisingly ended, as Adi Hütter returns to a club he last managed in 2021. Bayer Leverkusen removed Kasper Hjulmand from his position, opting for Spaniard Carles Martinez Novell who last coached at Toulouse. Perhaps the biggest coaching news is former Bayern Munich player Martin Demichelis taking over at RB Leipzig for Ole Werner, who was dismissed despite leading the club to third last season. Hamburg don't have a new coach, but in Kathleen Krüger they welcome a new Head of Sport who is not only breaking the glass ceiling but will give the club a new strategic vision moving forward.

Who are the new, exciting players to watch?

Dortmund’s Karetsas is an exciting, very talented player who was on the wish list of many clubs across Europe. The 18-year-old, who can play in attacking midfield and on the wing, joined Dortmund from KRC Genk this summer.

Nathan De Cat is one of the most exciting young Belgian players. The 18-year-old defensive midfielder joined Hoffenheim this summer, leaving Anderlecht.

A duo of young German prospects at newly promoted Elversberg is worth keeping an eye on: Francis Onyeka (on loan from Leverkusen) and Noah Darvich (on loan from Stuttgart) are considered two of the most exciting 19-year-old players in the country. They are expected to play a major role in Elversberg's debut Bundesliga season, and take big strides in their development in the process.

Germany’s arguably most sought-after talent, Kennet Eichhorn, who left Hertha Berlin for Bayer Leverkusen this summer, must first recover from an injury. The 16-year-old is currently battling a metabolic disorder that led to significant weight loss and physical weakness during preseason. His Bundesliga debut is most likely to come in 2027 as a result.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

entries.title: Nepal floods: More than 160 killed, nearly 1,400 missing
entries.summary: Rescue teams are searching for survivors after a glacial collapse triggered catastrophic floods in Nepal and Tibet. Hundreds of foreign tourists are missing.
entries.content:
Nepal

Nepal floods: More than 160 killed, nearly 1,400 missing

August 27, 2026

Rescue teams are searching for survivors after a glacial collapse triggered catastrophic floods in Nepal and Tibet. Hundreds of foreign tourists are missing.

The death toll from catastrophic flash floods along the border between Nepal and Tibet has risen to at least 165, while nearly 1,400 people were missing.

Rescue teams were searching for survivors on Thursday, a day after a glacial collapse sent a huge wall of mud and rock barreling through the Himalayan communities, sweeping way entire villages.

Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said 826 people were missing in the country, almost 600 of them foreign nationals.

In Tibet, Chinese broadcaster CCTV reported 558 people missing in Gyirong county, including 260 foreigners. Three deaths had been confirmed there as of Thursday morning, with two villagers rescued.

What do we know about the flood in Nepal and Tibet?

The disaster struck Wednesday when a glacial collapse triggered a flood in the Lhende Khola river, a tributary of the Bhotekoshi, in a corridor popular with trekkers and pilgrims connecting Kathmandu with Lhasa. 

Nepal police spokesperson Abi Narayan Kafle told Reuters the death toll was expected to keep climbing: "This will go up, as we have resumed the search and more bodies are expected to be recovered."

Among those missing in Nepal were large numbers of foreign tourists.

Sunil Sharma, a tourism board spokesperson, told the AP news agency that 133 of the missing were Indian pilgrims traveling to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a site sacred to Hindus, alongside 47 Americans, 34 Australians, 33 Britons and 24 Canadians.

Reuters cited a slightly different breakdown from police and tourism officials, putting the missing tourists at 177 from India, 63 from the United States, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada.

Survivors describe scale of destruction

As the scale of the disaster became apparent on Thursday, locals recounted a torrent of mud rushing toward them.

 

"As it got closer, it kept rising higher and higher. When I saw it enter our home, I tried to grab my wife's hand and take her to the terrace. But she was swept away by the mud," Keshav Prasad Baral, a 68-year-old survivor, told Reuters. 

He was rescued by helicopter four hours later. "My wife is still somewhere beneath the mud."

"She's gone," he said. 

 

Sagar Pandey, who heads a Himalayan tourism operator, surveyed the area by helicopter and saw that entire settlements had vanished.

 

"There are no human-made things, no human settlement left. Everything is just flat. So anyone in the hotel, the restaurant, or the car, I believe that everybody is gone," he told Reuters.

 

More than 5,000 army and police personnel have been mobilized in Nepal, according to army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet. They were using helicopters to drop supplies, including tents, food and more, donated by India to communities cut off by the disaster.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama dies at 97
entries.summary: From works of "self-obliteration" to polka dotted nudes, the pioneering artist developed a unique body of work likely to be relevant for years to come.
entries.content:
August 27, 2026

From works of "self-obliteration" to polka dotted nudes, the pioneering artist developed a unique body of work likely to be relevant for years to come.

Yayoi Kusama gained fame in recent years for her Instagramable "Infinity Rooms" — immersive installations using mirrors, lights and reflective surfaces to create the illusion of endless space — as well as her large-scale polka dot sculptures. While her works often appear playful, behind them lies the story of a woman who has faced major social and mental health challenges.

Around the age of 10, Yayoi Kusama began experiencing hallucinations, seeing dots and net patterns enveloping everything in her mind's eye. She attributed these early visions to the psychological strain of growing up with an unloving mother, who forbade her from painting and tried to impose traditional expectations on her behavior. Although she continued to experience hallucinations until late in life, Kusama learned to live with them and channel them into her art. "My artwork is an expression of my life, particularly of my mental disease," Kusama once told US arts publication Bomb Magazine.

After attending the Kyoto School of Arts and Crafts, Kusama held her first exhibitions in her hometown of Matsumoto. She was unusually open about her mental health at a time when such topics were heavily stigmatized.

"It was extraordinary that she addressed it so openly," said Stephan Diederich, curator of the Kusama retrospective at Cologne's Museum Ludwig which took place in 2026.

"For her, art was a survival strategy and a form of therapy, which she always made clear without making it the main focus," Diederich told DW.

Kusama's escape to New York

For Kusama, who was born on March 22, 1929, life in Japan soon became too stifling.

"[My parents] were always trying to rope me into arranged marriages with men I'd never met who came from very particular families," Yayoi once told writer Andrew Solomon, referring to her early 20s as "my era of mental breakdown." She increasingly felt like "a prisoner surrounded by a curtain of depersonalization."

Finally, she broke free from the conventions and expectations of postwar Japan and moved to New York in 1958. "She was exceptionally self-confident and determined to go her own way and pursue a career," said Diederich. Kusama's mother provided her with financial support to get started — on the condition that she never return to Japan. Fellow artist Georgia O'Keeffe, to whom Kusama had previously sent a selection of her works, helped her gain a foothold in the United States.

Kusama often spent entire days working and produced a vast body of art. She became part of the New York avant-garde scene, where her meticulous "Infinity Net" paintings drew attention for their hypnotic, repetitive patterns.

Her works, including soft, often phallic fabric sculptures, paralleled some of the approaches of contemporaries like Andy Warhol and Claes Oldenburg.

"She was very confident in saying that she set the benchmarks that her male colleagues later drew on," explained Diederich. However, he added, it's impossible to determine definitively who was first. In any case, her male fellow artists were more commercially successful than the young Asian woman, contributing to her attempted suicide, which she fortunately survived. Kusama made a statement about the gender pay gap with her sculpture "Traveling Life" (1964), which features a ladder covered in phallic shapes with women's shoes on the steps.

Phalluses are another recurring motif Kusama used to process her "fear of sex as something dirty," as she wrote in her 2022 autobiography. Returning to the universe through self-obliteration in the 1960s, Kusama held "happenings" as protests against the Vietnam War. They were often provocative, sometimes involving nudity and sexual activity, although Kusama often noted that she didn't personally participate in the sexual aspects of these events.

"Why should people who share pleasure with each other go to war and kill others? Through free sex, the wall between me and others can be torn down," Kusama wrote in her autobiography.

She was known for painting nude female and male bodies with dots, with the aim of erasing the individuality of those painted. She calls this "self-obliteration," and it runs through her entire body of work. "By obliterating one's self, you return to the infinite universe," Kusama once said.

In 1966, Kusama staged her work "Narcissus Garden" at the Venice Biennale. She placed 1,500 mirrored spheres on the lawn outside the entrance of the Venice Biennale, which she hadn't been invited to, and attempted to sell them for $2 each. Biennale officials eventually intervened and stopped the sale, but the work still served as a pointed critique of the commercialization of the art world and the role of artists in it.

Fame later in life

In 1993, Kusama returned to the Venice Biennale as an officially invited artist, representing Japan.

She later told the Financial Times that she wanted "to become more famous, even more famous," a remark that reflects how important recognition had become in her career and one that some commentators critiqued as overly focused on fame.

Over the past decade she reached a level of fame any artist would be envious of. In 2018, The Broad museum in Los Angeles quickly sold 90,000 advance tickets for a Kusama exhibition. A yearlong show at London's Tate Modern in 2022 sold out in no time, as did the one-year extension. Her artworks went on to fetch millions at auction.

Yayoi Kusama returned to Japan in 1973 and chose to live in a psychiatric clinic in Tokyo, where she received treatment for her mental health. She remained highly productive, creating paintings, sculptures, installations and other works that are exhibited around the world until her last days.

"I will continue to create artwork as long as my passion keeps me doing so. I am deeply moved that so many people have been my fans," she said in a previous interview. "I suppose I would not be able to know how people would evaluate my art until after I die. I create art for the healing of all mankind."

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: US Army to spend $2 billion nuclear microreactors for bases
entries.summary: The US Army has announced a plan to install what it calls nuclear microreactors at five of its bases across the country. The move would ensure the facilities' energy independence from the rest of the electric grid.
entries.content:
United States of America

US Army to spend $2 billion nuclear microreactors for bases

August 27, 2026

The US Army has announced a plan to install what it calls nuclear microreactors at five of its bases across the country. The move would ensure the facilities' energy independence from the rest of the electric grid.

The United States Army said Wednesday that it will award $2.2 billion (€1.7 billion) in contracts to five companies to build and operate small nuclear reactors on military bases. The program set a goal of deploying the first such reactor by the end of September 2028.

Called microreactors, developers say each of the nuclear plants would be easy to transport and provide up to 20 megawatts of power.

The reactors will adhere to all environmental and safety regulations that apply to commercial reactors, but an Army spokesperson said the reactors will be regulated by the Army rather than the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission, which regulates commercial reactors.

"The whole idea here is that at the back end of this we want a commercial product," said Jeff Waksman, principal deputy assistant secretary of the Army for Installations, Energy and Environment.

Army Secretary Dan Driscoll said the awards will speed up the military's ability "to deliver safe, reliable baseload power directly to our installations."

"We are building the energy resilience necessary to project combat power globally, without relying on potentially vulnerable external grids," he added.

What companies are involved?

The Army selected the following companies to work at its bases:

  • Antares Nuclear at Fort Bragg, North Carolina
  • BWXT Advanced Technologies ​at Fort Campbell, Kentucky
  • General Atomics Electromagnetic Systems at Fort Hood, Texas
  • Radiant ​Industries, Fort Benning, Georgia
  • Westinghouse Government Services at Fort Drum, New York

Radiant's Chief Commercial Officer Mike Starrett told Reuters news agency that the project, called Janus, will help the company scale up its business to meet the needs of commercial customers, like data centers, in about 2030.

Rex Geveden, president and chief executive officer of BWXT, said, "As we commence work on the Janus program, we are delivering the nation's most credible and reliable path to deployable nuclear power."

'Hidden subsidy' for expensive reactors, critics say

Critics of microreactors say they will be expensive compared to conventional reactors. Safety advocates point out that nuclear technology carries significant risks that other low-carbon energy sources don't, such as the danger of accidents or targeted attacks.

The Army program uses the military's "deep pockets to provide a hidden subsidy" to nuclear companies that can't find private-sector customers for their hypothetical and uneconomical reactors, Alan J. Kuperman, associate professor at the Lyndon B. Johnson School of Public Affairs at the University of Texas at Austin and coordinator of the Nuclear Proliferation Prevention Project, told the AP news agency.

The Army's Waksman said nobody thinks that microreactors will be lower in cost than conventional plants.

"What we are trying to do here with Janus ... is to flesh out how can we get those prices down," he said.

What will happen with the radioactive waste?

Waksman said the microreactors would safely shut down in case of a failure and that the Army wouldn't add them to installations without being certain they are safe.

He added that the Army is working on a deal with the Energy Department to remove radioactive waste, and there won't be any long-term storage on these installations.

Last month, five states offered to accept nuclear waste in exchange for federal support in developing nuclear energy facilities.

Trump pushing nuclear power in US

Executive orders signed by US President Donald Trump in May 2025 aimed to accelerate the development of nuclear power. Trump has called for the US to quadruple its nuclear energy production — just two new large reactors have been built from scratch in the United States in nearly 50 years. Those two reactors were completed years late and at least $17 billion over budget, AP reported.

The nation's 94 nuclear reactors supply about 19% of U.S. electricity, compared to about 60% for fossil fuels and 21% for renewables, according to the US Energy Information Administration.

Edited by: Kieran Burke

entries.title: France: Car rams crowd at bus stop in Caen
entries.summary: At least one person was killed and several injured when a car drove into a bus shelter in the northern French city of Caen.
entries.content:
August 27, 2026

At least one person was killed and several injured when a car drove into a bus shelter in the northern French city of Caen.

A person drove a car into a crowd in the northwestern French city of Caen on Wednesday, killing at least one person and injuring about a dozen others, firefighters and police said, according to the AFP news agency and BFM TV.

A police source said the driver rammed the car into the crowd near the city's train station after a fight in the area, and one suspect was arrested, AFP reported.

BFM TV reported that two people had been killed in the incident.

The driver fled and was later arrested 20 kilometers (12 miles) away, a source told AFP.

The incident occurred around 10:00 p.m. local time (2000 UTC/GMT) near a bus stop close to the Caen train station. According to initial reports, a black vehicle drove into several people who were in the area.

Police cordoned off the area while emergency services attended to the victims.

Authorities are investigating the circumstances of the incident and trying to determine whether the attack was intentional.

Edited by: Kieran Burke

entries.title: Ukraine airstrike on bus in Russian-occupied Luhansk kills 9
entries.summary: Russian authorities in the occupied territory say the drone attack caused injuries. Kyiv also destroyed another Wildberries warehouse.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine airstrike on bus in Russian-occupied Luhansk kills 9

August 26, 2026

Russian authorities in the occupied territory say the drone attack caused injuries. Kyiv also destroyed another Wildberries warehouse.

A Ukrainian airstrike killed nine people in Ukraine's eastern, Russian-occupied Luhansk region on Wednesday, according to Leonid Pasechnik, leader of Russia's occupying forces there.

Pasechnik labeled the strike "a war crime," saying it had killed eight people on the spot and that another person, a 20-year-old woman, died of her injuries shortly thereafter.

The bus was said to have been carrying 15 people, with five more reported injured.

Ukraine keeps up strikes in Russia, destroys another major warehouse

With US-brokered peace talks failing to get off the ground and the Kremlin sticking to its maximalist demands before agreeing to end its four-and-a-half-year invasion, Kyiv and Moscow have continued to escalate their air campaigns.

Kyiv again targeted logistics infrastructure on Wednesday, using drones to destroy another Wildberries warehouse, this one in Russia's Tambov region, southeast of Moscow.

Tambov's governor said the 100,000 square-meter (1.1 million square-foot) facility — an area roughly the size of 14 soccer fields — had been "completely destroyed by fire."

Wildberries is Russia's biggest online retailer.

Ukrainian strikes on its facilities not only disrupt the Kremlin's military logistics — Kyiv says Wildberries aids the military war effort — they also strike at Russia's civilian economy and thus touch everyday Russians.

This week, Kyiv expanded its target list to include Russia's number two online retailer, Ozon.

In an analysis of satellite imagery, Reuters news agency estimated that at least 1.9 ​million square meters of warehouse space had been severely damaged in Ukrainian drone attacks on more than 20 Wildberries and Ozon facilities in recent weeks.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: No, this wasn't a "completely normal summer", despite far-right climate denial
entries.summary: Some political messaging denies the role of human-caused climate change in this summer's extreme heat. The science tells a different story.
entries.content:
August 26, 2026

Some political messaging denies the role of human-caused climate change in this summer's extreme heat. The science tells a different story.

As a summer of European extreme heat draws to a close, politicians are looking back at the toll. Germany recordedaround 14,000 heat-related deaths, almost two-thirds in one scorching week of June alone. A Dutch bank estimated summer heat will cost the EU €180 billion ($209 billion) in lost GDP. And in June, European farmers lost approximately 9 million tons in grain crops. 

Climate change, long a politically charged topic, has become a daily reality for people around the world. These effects and more are making it increasingly difficult to challenge what people are seeing with their own eyes.

Yet that hasn't stopped the global populist right from trying. Richard Tice, deputy leader of the UK's far-right Reform Party said "climate change has always happened, it always will," adding that it was arrogant to try to stop it. He encouraged the British public to enjoy the heat.

In the United States, Harriet Hageman, a Republican politician and potentially Wyoming's next senator, told far-right channel Real America's Voice that Europe’s heatwave was business as usual. "It's called summer. Some years are hotter than others and some years are colder than others," she said. "But that's just the cyclical nature of weather."

And Tino Chrupalla, co-leader of Germany’s far-right AfD party told a journalist in recent days that it's been a "completely normal summer." He dismissed climate change as "hype." 

 

But claims like these don't stand up to scientific scrutiny.

As NASA statesplainly: "Scientific evidence continues to show that human activities (primarily the human burning of fossil fuels) have warmed Earth's surface and its ocean basins, which in turn have continued to impact Earth’s climate."

This was not 'a completely normal summer'

This summer has been historically hot. Independent climate monitoring bodies, including the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) in the US, the Copernicus Climate Change Service in the European Union and the Japan Meterological Agency, all called last month either the joint-warmest or joint-second warmest month on record.

The conditions have led energy plants to halt production, outdated concrete motorways blowing up, and older buildings overheating during the day and barely cooling down at night — threatening inhabitants with exposure to heat stress.

The extreme heat was felt almost everywhere on the globe. According to NOAA's data, it was the warmest July ever for North America, Africa and Asia.

The continental United States just surpassedits warmest July records. They were previously set in 1936, during the infamous Dust Bowl that scorched the US Great Plains with extreme temperatures, and in 2012, when North America suffered an extreme heatwave.

And the daily average sea surface temperature hitits highest level since records began in 1979 — reaching 21.1 degrees Celsius (70 degrees Fahrenheit) this month. That's a result of both human-driven warming as well as El Nino, a climate cycle that weakens trade winds and warms tropical Pacific surface temperatures.

How climate change supercharged this summer's fires

In Spain, the far-right Vox party saidfires — which burned more than 254,000 hectares of land across the country this season — were not connected to climate change. 

Yet experts agree rising global temperatures played a major role in the intense wildfire season that also scorched large parts of France and Canada. That's because extreme heat creates ideal conditions for wildfires to start and spread.

A field of climate research called attribution science explores the extent to which climate change exacerbates extreme weather events like this summer's wildfires. Using models, researchers compare the likelihood and intensity of an event in today's climate with a simulated world in which there is no human-caused warming.

Analyses done this summer showthat hotter global temperatures created conditions that made the wildfires in Spain 20 times more likely to happen, and twice as probable in France.

This is due to a phenomenon known as weather whiplash, where ecosystems swing dramatically between wet and dry conditions.

When the planet warms, the atmosphere holds more moisture, rainfall is intensified, and plants grow. Then, in summer, that same warm atmosphere draws water from soil and plants, worsening drought and drying out vegetation, turning it into the perfect fuel for fires.

"We know — and this is mathematically proven — that the probability of having fire weather that can sustain and create this kind of event has been altered by climate change," Francesca Di Giuseppe, a fire forecast project coordinator at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, told DW about this summer's fires in Spain and France.

Climate change's ripple effects

Overall, this summer has left its mark in numerous ways that are impossible to ignore.

Bodies of water across Europe are drying out under the intense heat. Parts of the Rhine, Danube and Po rivers have fallen to historically low levels, making it impossible for ships to pass through in some spots.

This has a number of knock-on effects. Drinking water costs could rise dramatically as much of Germany's clean water first passes through reed-filled riverbanks that are crucial for filtration.

Supply chains are also be disrupted, as vessels can't carry as much cargo when water levels are lower, increasing prices across the economy in products like steel or petroleum.

In America, drought conditions are wreaking havoc on crops and livestock. In June, the US Department of Agriculture said the 10-month stretch from August 2025 to May 2026 was the nation's driest period since 1976-77. 

Now, 59% of the country's sorghum is being grown in areas experiencing drought. More than half the nation's cattle production and almost two-thirds of spring wheat production is happening under water scarcity.

Such conditions can put direct strain on the country's food supply, increase prices and threaten rural livelihoods.

By any measurement — thermometers, drought maps, or death tolls — and in much of the world, this summer has been historically extreme.

Edited by: Tamsin Walker

entries.title: Tim Curry, of 'The Rocky Horror Picture Show,' dies at 80
entries.summary: The gender-bending role as Dr. Frank-N-Furter put Curry on the map in 1975. He then went on to play a number of villainous roles like Gomez Addams, Pennywise and Bill Sikes, but also Mozart and William Shakespeare.
entries.content:
August 26, 2026

The gender-bending role as Dr. Frank-N-Furter put Curry on the map in 1975. He then went on to play a number of villainous roles like Gomez Addams, Pennywise and Bill Sikes, but also Mozart and William Shakespeare.

Actor Tim Curry died at the age of 80, Variety, TMZ and other celebrity news outlets reported on Wednesday.

A cause of death was not immediately given but Curry had been in poor health for some time following a severe stroke that left him confined to a wheelchair and wrote in his memoir "Vagabond" last year that he was still not able to walk.

Curry won Laurence Olivier and Tony Award nominations for his work on stage in the UK and the US, as well delivering Emmy-winning TV performances later in his career.

Who was Tim Curry?

Curry was born in Cheshire into a Navy family in 1946 and spent his life bouncing around an array of different homes in the UK and even Hong Kong. He ultimately went to school in Bath, impressing as a soprano singer, and university in Birmingham.

He played in London musicals in the late 60s and early 70s seeking his big break, which came in a 1973 unusual musical ultimately destined to graduate to the silver screen.

Curry was given the role of the lingerie-clad sweet singing transvestite Dr. Frank-N-Furter in the cult classic film "The Rocky Horror Picture Show" in 1975. Despite the very German sounding name and initial rehearsals with a German and American accent, he ultimately played the mad scientist with an exaggerated upper class Belgravia accent, in what a Guardian newspaper 1973 review referred to as a "garishly Bowiesque performance as the ambisextrous doctor."

He went on to play an array of other roles that involved elaborate costumes, unusual mannerisms, and often a fairly pronounced dark but also comedic side in his career.

These included Gomez Addams in the "Addams Family Reunion" cinema reboot, Long John Silver in "Muppet Treasure Island," the suspicious Plaza Hotel concierge in "Home Alone 2: Lost in New York," Pennywise the Clown in a miniseries based on Stephen King's novel "It," and even as the voice of Chancellor Palpatine in "Star Wars: The Clone Wars."

In another Star Wars connection, Curry was even cast as the Joker for "Batman: The Animated Series," having been considered for the role in the 1989 film as well, until Mark Hamill supplanted him.

Curry also played some of history's most consequential figures like Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, William Shakespeare, and even King Arthur — albeit in the Monty Python musical stage show "Spamalot." He was also among the first actors to branch out into video game roles, perhaps most notably as the fictional Soviet military officer Anatoly Cherdenko in Command and Conquer: Red Alert 3.

He released several solo studio albums and also contributed to various soundtrack records throughout his career, with his musical background apparent in many of his acting roles.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: This extremely successful author polarizes German readers
entries.summary: She's young and she says what she thinks: Caroline Wahl is topping Germany's bestseller lists with her novels. But she has also faced public backlash.
entries.content:
August 26, 2026

She's young and she says what she thinks: Caroline Wahl is topping Germany's bestseller lists with her novels. But she has also faced public backlash.

Caroline Wahl, 31, has published three novels to date. All three shot to the top of Germany's fiction bestseller lists.

Now, her fourth book is set to be released on August 28: "1999 Meter über dem Meer" (1999 Meters Above Sea) tells the story of a young woman who takes on a false identity to mingle among the high society in St. Moritz, Switzerland.

It is one of the most anticipated new books of the summer in Germany.

So what is the secret to Caroline Wahl's success?

Debut with a bang

Caroline Wahl's breakthrough came with her first novel, from 2023: "22 Bahnen" (22 Lengths) sold more than a million copies in German-language editions.

The story of the young student Tilda, who has to navigate everyday life alongside her alcoholic mother and her little sister, was praised by critics for its straightforward, modern writing style.

What's more, the novel managed to fascinate readers across generations: It includes references to contemporary pop culture as well as to classic literature.

"The many references make the novels both diverse and ambiguous," says Matthias Schaffrick, a research associate at the Collaborative Research Center "Transformations of the Popular" at the University of Siegen, who recently organized a two-day symposium on Wahl's works.

"What stands out most is how she experiments with different narrative styles and questions them, instead of simply telling a story," Shaffrick tells DW. "This opens up a literary space with multiple possibilities, enabling different interpretations and certainly contributing to the appeal of her novels for many readers."

Polarizing ambition

The success led to the media becoming interested in the young author, and quickly showed that Caroline Wahl does not care much for conventions: She speaks her mind freely and doesn't mind facing backlash. "I enjoy being polarizing," she told the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper last weekend. "I like that there's no gray area, people either hate me, and then they really hate me (...). Or they like me."

In the podcast "Hotel Matze," she said she wanted to become one of Germany's most famous authors. Her words quickly created a stir, but Wahl didn't mind: "I'm really not up for false modesty. It's not wrong to state your goals ambitiously," she said on the arts and culture TV show "Twist" on the Arte channel. "For young women in particular, it's more extreme than for men — people get irritated when a young woman says, 'I want to be the best.' I want to change that with my attitude."     

A passion for fast cars

Part of that is openly speaking about enjoying her newfound wealth. In an interview with SZ-Magazin, she said: "It's not only the writing that is enjoyable, but also being successful. Financial success is also important." She loves fast cars, drives a convertible and bought a camper van she likes to park somewhere with a view of the sea to work.

On social media, she faced a lot of criticism. She has been accused of making money off the literary depiction of poverty in "22 Bahnen," despite never having lived an impoverished life herself. It's an age-old discussion about whether authors are only allowed to write about things they have experienced themselves. Wahl replied to this criticism on the Deutschlandfunk radio station, explaining that above all, writing to her means "exploring spaces that I don't know and feeling empathy for people who live a different life than mine."

But even without the debate on her credibility, a young woman who speaks openly about material success still seems to be unsettling for many people in Germany — men and women alike — as the many negative reactions show. To Wahl herself, the debate is misogynist.

On Instagram, she wrote a caption for a photo of her light blue BMW: "I find it weird and don't quite get why it's cool for rappers or other men to show off their AMGs, etc., but when a woman author wants to buy a sports car (and can afford to do so!!!), people advise her not to do it and more importantly, not to show it in public."

Author and influencer

"What happens when something becomes very popular?" asks literary scholar Matthias Schaffrick: "The popularity starts being scrutinized, which you can observe in Caroline Wahl's case. And we can see what it means to be a popular author. It's not only her novels that play a role, but also the persona she creates for herself as an author."

By being active on Instagram, where she has even tested energy drinks, she also taps into the role of an influencer, says Matthias Schaffrick. "It makes her even more popular and offers new topics for conversation. At the same time, the public debate shifts the focus away from her literature, which is what's actually interesting about the Caroline Wahl phenomenon."

Wahl herself admits that the intensity of the backlash and criticism has hurt her. In an interview with the SWR TV channel, she explained that social criticism is not necessarily her intention. "I'm not trying to change anything with my stories. Above all, I want to tell stories."

'22 Lengths' on school curricula

When it comes to best‑sellers, opinions always differ among German literary critics: Is this entertaining literature, or serious literature with high artistic aspirations? The arts and feature sections of numerous newspapers come to different conclusions on whether Caroline Wahl's novels can be classified as part of the latter. In an interview with Spiegel, Wahl said she finds "drawing a line between entertaining and serious simply annoying."

So far, Wahl's novels have not been nominated for the German Book Prize, Germany's highest literature award. In 2024, the writer voiced her disappointment in typical fashion on Instagram: "I'm sad and angry that I have not been included on the longlist, even if I somehow knew this would happen. Too successful, says my agent."

Back then, her debut novel could have been included on the list — a book that was quickly added to school curricula and has now been made into a film.

Likewise, on this year's longlist, Wahl's novel "Die Assistentin" (The Assistant) has not been included. A literature critic from Frankfurter Rundschau had this to say about the decision: "Why is good literature always supposed to hurt before it can be deemed 'valuable'? (...) The fact that an author like Wahl has been ignored, simply because her captivating writing fascinates millions of readers, makes me really angry."

Presumably, Caroline Wahl's fans will ensure that her new novel becomes another bestseller — even without the German Book Prize.
